youtube_title: Ireland's Supreme Court Said Subway's Bread Isn't Bread (for Tax) 🦝⚖️
caption: In Bookfinders v Revenue Commissioners (2020), Ireland's Supreme Court held the Subway bread at issue exceeded the VAT law's 2% sugar limit for 'bread', so it didn't qualify for the zero rate.
script: A Supreme Court officially ruled that Subway bread has too much sugar to legally be bread. [disclaimer] Yes, really! Here's the background. In Ireland, real bread gets a special zero percent tax. But the law is super picky about what counts as bread. Stuff like sugar and fat can't be more than two percent of the weight of the flour. A Subway franchise owner wanted a tax refund from two thousand four and two thousand five, for its bread, hot sandwiches, tea and coffee. The tax office said no. So the company fought it. And lost. Then lost again. And again. All the way up to the Supreme Court, in twenty twenty. So what was the problem? The sugar! Subway's recipe had sugar at about ten percent of the flour's weight. That's five times the limit! And the court said if even one ingredient goes over, it's not bread under the law. Tax breaks are read strictly. Period. And the hot sandwich argument? It failed too, because it needed the bread to count first. So the headlines screamed, Subway bread isn't bread! More exactly, this recipe didn't fit Ireland's tax definition of bread.
